## Overview

This division funds Congress itself and the agencies that support it for fiscal year 2016 (October 1, 2015–September 30, 2016). It pays for the House and Senate, the Capitol Police, the Architect of the Capitol, the Library of Congress, the Government Accountability Office, the Congressional Budget Office, and the Government Publishing Office. Its purpose is to keep the legislative branch running: member offices, committees, security, buildings, research, audits, and public access to government information.

## Total Spending

The text does not print one grand total. Adding the appropriation lines comes to about **$4.41 billion**. Roughly **$42.1 million** of the Library of Congress and Copyright Office totals is expected to come from fees rather than the Treasury, so the net draw on taxpayers is about **$4.36 billion**. The bill does not compare these amounts with the prior year. The Government Accountability Office may also use an extra **$25.5 million** in payments it receives, on top of its main appropriation.

## Key Funding Areas

- **House of Representatives**: $1.18 billion — salaries and expenses for members, committees, leadership, and House officers.
- **Members’ Representational Allowances (House)**: $554.3 million — staff, district office costs, and official mail for representatives, delegates, and the resident commissioner.
- **Senate**: $870.2 million — leadership offices, officers, committees, and contingent expenses.
- **Senators’ Official Personnel and Office Expense Account**: $390 million — staff and office costs for senators.
- **Architect of the Capitol**: $612.9 million — upkeep of the Capitol, office buildings, grounds, power plant, Botanic Garden, and Capitol Visitor Center. Includes $62 million, available until spent, for renovation of the Cannon House Office Building, plus $10 million for the House Historic Buildings Revitalization Trust Fund.
- **Library of Congress**: $642.0 million gross (about $599.9 million after fee offsets) — the library’s operations, the Copyright Office ($58.9 million, mostly fee-funded), the Congressional Research Service ($106.9 million), and Books for the Blind and Physically Handicapped ($50.2 million).
- **Government Accountability Office**: $531 million — audits and investigations for Congress.
- **U.S. Capitol Police**: $375 million — $309 million for salaries (overtime capped at $30.9 million unless the appropriations committees are notified) and $66 million for equipment, training, and other costs.
- **Senate inquiries and investigations**: $133.3 million — committee investigations; $26.7 million available through September 30, 2018.
- **Government Publishing Office**: $117.1 million — congressional printing ($79.7 million), public document distribution ($30.5 million), and technology and building repairs ($6.8 million).
- **Congressional Budget Office**: $46.5 million — nonpartisan budget and cost estimates for Congress.

Smaller items include the Joint Committee on Taxation ($10.1 million), the Office of the Attending Physician ($3.8 million), the Office of Compliance ($4.0 million), the 2017 inaugural ceremonies ($1.25 million), the Open World Leadership Center ($5.6 million), and the John C. Stennis Center ($430,000).

## Notable Provisions

- Leftover House member office allowances, and unspent Senate office-account money after its availability period, must go back to the Treasury for deficit reduction, or for debt reduction if there is no deficit.
- House offices do not automatically get printed bills, the Congressional Record, the Daily Calendar, the Congressional Pictorial Directory, or House disbursement reports. Printed copies of the U.S. Code for the whole House are capped at 50 of any edition.
- A House member’s office allowance may not be used to lease a vehicle for more than $1,000 a month, not counting mobile district offices.
- The Architect of the Capitol may not pay incentive awards to contractors who are behind schedule or over budget, unless the delay or overrun is unforeseeable, caused by the government, or not significant.
- No funds may be used for photo “scrims” (printed images of building fronts) during Architect restoration projects.
- The Architect may acquire about 7.34 acres at Fort Meade, Maryland, from the state highway administration at no cost to the United States.
- The Capitol Police may keep reimbursements for help at events that Congress did not sponsor. Basic training at the Federal Law Enforcement Training Center is paid by the Department of Homeland Security, not this bill.
- Member- and staff-led guided tours of the Capitol cannot be eliminated with these funds, except for temporary security restrictions approved through the Capitol Police Board.
- The House Wounded Warrior Program receives $2.5 million, available until spent. The Office of Congressional Ethics receives $1.5 million.
- Outgoing Librarian of Congress James H. Billington may use the honorary title Librarian of Congress Emeritus and receive incidental support; it is not a paid federal appointment.
- Open World funds for Russian participants may be used only for free-market development, humanitarian work, and civic engagement—not for officials of Russia’s central government.
- The Architect may install electric-vehicle charging stations in Library of Congress parking only if users’ fees cover the cost, with approval from the Joint Committee on the Library.
- The Senate Chaplain may shift money between salary and expense accounts. GAO may accept staff detailed from other federal offices.

## Who Benefits

Primary beneficiaries are members of Congress and their staff, through office budgets, committees, and support offices. Capitol Police, the Attending Physician, and accessibility services protect and serve people who work in or visit the Capitol complex. The public benefits through the Library of Congress, free library service for blind and print-disabled readers ($650,000 of that account is specifically for newspapers), depository libraries served by the Government Publishing Office, and the Capitol Visitor Center ($20.6 million). Taxpayers benefit indirectly from GAO audits and CBO cost estimates. The House Wounded Warrior Program supports wounded veterans working in House offices. Open World supports international civic and leadership exchanges, with the Russia restriction noted above.

## Plain English Summary

This is the part of the 2016 spending bill that pays for Congress and the people and buildings around it—about $4.4 billion before fee offsets, closer to $4.36 billion after Library and Copyright fees are counted. Most of the money goes to House and Senate offices and staff, Capitol security, fixing and running the Capitol complex (including a big renovation of the Cannon House Office Building), the Library of Congress, and the watchdogs who audit federal programs and estimate what bills cost. The fine print trims automatic paper deliveries, sends unused member office money back toward the deficit, blocks bonuses for contractors who miss deadlines or bust budgets, and sets aside smaller sums for things like Capitol tours, the 2017 inauguration, books for blind readers, and a House program for wounded veterans.

## Title Summary

Title II sets cross-cutting rules for the Legislative Branch appropriations in this Act (fiscal year 2016). It does not create new program accounts; it limits how those funds may be used, makes certain pay and expense provisions permanent law, and grants ongoing authorities to the Architect of the Capitol, the Library of Congress, and the Government Publishing Office.

## Spending Breakdown

This title contains no new appropriations. The only dollar figure in the text is a cap on shared administrative costs.

| Line Item | Amount | Purpose |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| Legislative Branch Financial Managers Council (LBFMC) shared costs (Sec. 205) | Not to exceed $2,000 total | Caps the combined share of LBFMC administrative costs that participating legislative branch entities may finance from their administrative funds |
| Battery recharging stations, Library of Congress parking (Sec. 209) | No new appropriation; existing “Capitol Power Plant” funds, reimbursable | Authorizes construction, operation, and maintenance of chargers for privately owned vehicles, with user fees required to cover costs so there is no net federal cost |
| All other sections | No dollar amounts | Restrictions, permanent-law designations, or authorities that do not appropriate funds |

## Notable Sections

- **Sec. 201** bars use of these funds for maintenance or care of private vehicles, except emergency assistance and cleaning under House and Senate parking rules.
- **Sec. 202** provides that funds in this Act expire at the end of fiscal year 2016 unless the Act expressly says otherwise.
- **Sec. 203** makes rates of compensation and position designations in this Act permanent law where they differ from the Legislative Pay Act of 1929, and does the same for official expenses of Members, officers, and committees and for clerk hire.
- **Sec. 204** requires consulting-service contracts paid from this Act to be a matter of public record, with limited exceptions under existing law or executive order.
- **Sec. 206** permanently authorizes the Architect of the Capitol, in consultation with the District of Columbia, to maintain and improve landscape features (not streets) in Square 580 up to the start of I–395, beginning in fiscal year 2016.
- **Sec. 207** prohibits transfers of these funds to other federal entities except under transfer authority in this Act or another appropriations act.
- **Sec. 208** prohibits using Architect of the Capitol funds to eliminate or restrict guided Capitol tours led by employees and interns of Member and other House and Senate offices, while allowing temporary suspension or restriction for security at the direction of the Capitol Police Board.
- **Sec. 209** authorizes battery recharging stations in Library of Congress parking at no net cost to the government: fees must cover costs, construction and fee changes need Joint Committee on the Library approval, and the Architect must report every three years on whether users are receiving a taxpayer subsidy and adjust rates if so. The authority is permanent.
- **Sec. 210** amends 5 U.S.C. § 5307(d) so the Librarian of Congress, the Architect of the Capitol, and the Director of the Government Publishing Office—not the executive-branch process—certify the performance appraisal systems used for their senior-level employees in connection with aggregate pay limits.

## Plain English

These provisions police how Congress’s own 2016 operating money may be spent—blocking most private-car upkeep, keeping staff-led Capitol tours, and allowing Library parking chargers only if employees pay the full cost.
